title: Explaining Grokking and Information Bottleneck through Neural Collapse Emergence
claim: Distinct late-phase phenomena share one underlying cause: contraction of within-class variance, which is tied to neural collapse through a chain of theorems.
layout: Hub-and-spoke diagram, 3 clusters. Grokking and information-bottleneck plots on the left, a class-variance cluster in the center, neural collapse on the right. Colored arrows are labeled with theorem numbers.
description: A conceptual map linking theory results. At the left, two small schematic plots show the phenomena. Top left is a grokking plot of accuracy against time, with a blue training curve that rises early and a red test curve that rises later. Below it is an information-bottleneck plane, I(Z;X) against I(Z;Y), with a black curve running from Phase 1 fitting to Phase 2 compression. In the center, four colored Gaussian blobs (orange, blue, green, purple) are joined at a central point and labeled 'Population Within-Class Variance'. At the right, four clusters of scattered dots in the same colors are labeled 'Neural Collapse'. Red and blue arrows labeled Theorem 3.2, 3.4, 4.1 and 4.3 connect the elements. A rounded box at the top right splits the story into Phase 1 (fitting the training set) and Phase 2 (neural collapse). The eye goes first to the left plots, then follows the arrows rightward.
caption: Conceptual relationships in the late-phase training discussed in this work.
abstract: The training dynamics of deep neural networks often defy expectations, even as these models form the foundation of modern machine learning. Two prominent examples are grokking, where test performance improves abruptly long after the training loss has plateaued, and the information bottleneck principle, where models progressively discard input information irrelevant to the prediction task as training proceeds. However, the mechanisms underlying these phenomena and their relations remain poorly understood. In this work, we present a unified explanation of such late-phase phenomena through the lens of neural collapse, which characterizes the geometry of learned representations. We show that the contraction of population within-class variance is a key factor underlying both grokking and information bottleneck, and relate this measure to the neural collapse measure defined on the training set. By analyzing the dynamics of neural collapse, we show that distinct time scales between fitting the training set and the progression of neural collapse account for the behavior of the late-phase phenomena. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings on multiple datasets and architectures.
